Chapter 4: Meeting Difficult Emotions with Openness
You know, difficult emotions are just part of being human. We all feel anger, fear, jealousy, or resentment now and then—sometimes when we least expect it. Most of us try to push those feelings away, distract ourselves, or fix them as quickly as possible. But what if, instead of fighting them, we met these emotions with a little openness and curiosity?
Let me share a story. There was a woman who used to dread family gatherings because old conflicts kept coming up. Every time, she’d feel that familiar mix of anger and sadness, and her first reaction was to either withdraw or argue. But one year, she tried something different. When those old feelings surfaced, she stopped, took a breath, and let herself really feel them—without judging or blaming anyone. She noticed the tightness in her chest, the heat in her face, and all the stories spinning in her mind.
Rather than acting on that emotion, she just stayed with it—breathing, observing. The feelings didn’t magically disappear, but they did become less overwhelming. She realized that beneath her anger was something softer—a longing to be understood and accepted. By meeting her emotions openly, she found a deep well of compassion for herself and even her family.
Most of us are taught to avoid discomfort at all costs. With our phones, TVs, and endless to-do lists, it’s easy to run away from tough feelings. But here’s something to pay attention to: when we avoid our emotions, they actually tighten their grip on us—making it more likely they’ll burst out in ways we don’t expect.
Meeting emotions with openness doesn’t mean acting them out or letting them take over. It’s about allowing them to be there, just as they are, without rushing to change or fix them. Sure, it takes courage and patience, and it’s not always comfortable, but this approach is deeply healing.
I remember hearing about a teacher who led a group through a meditation on anger. Everyone was asked to recall a recent moment of frustration and notice what was happening in their body, their mind, and their heart. The instruction was simple: just stay with the experience, breathe, and watch. Some people found it tough; they wanted to run away or judge themselves. Others felt a surprising sense of relief from just being present with their feelings.
Over time, this kind of practice reveals a powerful truth: emotions aren’t permanent. They show up, they peak, and eventually, they fade. When you meet them with openness, their intensity softens, your mind gets a little more spacious, and that urge to react starts to fade away—replaced by understanding and acceptance.
This new way of relating to emotions doesn’t just change your experience—it changes your relationships, too. When you can sit with your own anger or pain, you’re less likely to throw it at the people around you. Compassion grows—for yourself, and for others who are also struggling.
The real journey isn’t about never having difficult emotions. It’s about learning to meet them with kindness and curiosity, and trusting that, in time, they’ll pass. Every time you choose openness over avoidance, you take one small step toward greater freedom and peace.
